data.text:
## Overview

The only Supreme Court decision on geofence warrants in this corpus is *Chatrie v. United States*, decided June 29, 2026. Everything below comes from it. Lower-court rulings and state law are outside the corpus.

## What the Court described a geofence warrant to be

Investigators may draw a "geofence"—a virtual perimeter—around a crime scene and get a warrant compelling a company to hand over data about the cell phones located in that area near the time of the crime.

citations.cited_text: They may draw a "geofence"—a virtual perimeter—around the crime scene and get a warrant compelling a company to hand over data about the cell phones located in that area near the time of the crime.

data.text: The warrant in *Chatrie*
was directed to Google, and used to solve a bank robbery.

citations.cited_text: The geofence warrant at issue here was directed to Google, and used to solve a bank robbery.

data.text: It sought Location History data, a service that
records the location of a user's cell phone every two minutes or so.

citations.cited_text: Hundreds of millions of Google users have activated a service called Location History, which records the location of a user's cell phone every two minutes or so.

data.text:
The majority described a three-step protocol that Google developed with law enforcement:
-
At the first step, Google produces anonymized location data for all devices within the geofence during a specified timeframe.

citations.cited_text: At the first step, Google produces anonymized (i.e., no names attached) location data for all cell phones (or other devices) within the geofence—typically, a circle with a designated radius surrounding a latitude/longitude coordinate—during a specified timeframe.

data.text: At the second step, officials review that data and typically ask for additional information on a subset of still-anonymized users.

citations.cited_text: At the second step of the process, officials review the data produced and typically ask Google to provide additional information for a subset of still-anonymized users.

data.text: That data usually covers a longer timeframe and shows the user's location outside as well as inside the geofence.

citations.cited_text: That new data is usually for a longer timeframe than first specified; it also shows the user's location outside, as well as inside, the geofence.

data.text: At the third step, officials demand the identities of a further subset of users—their names, email addresses, and phone numbers.

citations.cited_text: Finally, at the third step, officials demand the identities of a further subset of users—their names, email addresses, and phone numbers.

data.text: The warrant here followed that pattern.
Google first gave up anonymized data for 19 users,

citations.cited_text: At the first stage of the process, Google gave up anonymized data for 19 users found within the geofence during the hour within which the robbery occurred.

data.text: officers winnowed the list to nine,

citations.cited_text: At the second stage, the officers winnowed the list to nine users.

data.text: and
then to three, whose identifying information Google supplied.

citations.cited_text: At the third and last step, the police again narrowed the list, this time to three users.

data.text: The majority noted the technique's growth:
Google received its first geofence warrant in 2016,

citations.cited_text: Google received its first geofence warrant in 2016.

data.text: 982 two years later, and more than 11,000 two years after that.

citations.cited_text: Two years later, it received 982; and two years after that, more than 11,000.

data.text:
## The holding (majority opinion, Justice Kagan)

The majority opinion is by Justice Kagan, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Sotomayor, Kavanaugh, and Jackson. It framed the question in two parts:
whether the police conducted a Fourth Amendment "search" when they acquired the data and, if so, whether that search was reasonable given the features of the warrant.

citations.cited_text: Answering that question in full would mean deciding whether the police conducted a Fourth Amendment "search" when they acquired the cell-phone data leading to Chatrie's arrest and, if so, whether that search was reasonable given the features of the warrant they employed.

data.text:
It decided only the first part.

>
[P]olice officers invade a cell-phone user's reasonable expectation of privacy when they access his Location History.

citations.cited_text: For all those reasons, we hold that police officers invade a cell-phone user's reasonable expectation of privacy when they access his Location History.

data.text: It does not matter that the time period scrutinized was only two hours, or that a third-party tech company handed over the materials.

citations.cited_text: It does not matter if the time period scrutinized was only two hours. Nor does it matter that the materials obtained were handed over by a third-party tech company.

data.text:
### Reasoning

- **Carpenter applies.** The majority said
everything *Carpenter* relied on to find a search when officers accessed carriers' CSLI records "applies as well or better" to Google's Location History data.

citations.cited_text: Everything Carpenter relied on to find that law enforcement officers conducted a Fourth Amendment search when they accessed wireless carriers' CSLI records applies as well or better to the police's accessing of Google's Location History data.

data.text: - **Precision.**
CSLI placed Carpenter within a sector ranging from one-eighth to four square miles, whereas Location History pinpointed Chatrie within around twenty meters.

citations.cited_text: Here is one way of comparing the two: At any given time, CSLI placed Carpenter within a "sector ranging from one-eighth to four square miles," whereas Location History pinpointed Chatrie's location within around twenty meters, which is less than two percent of a mile.

data.text: Unlike CSLI, Location History can also estimate a phone's elevation.

citations.cited_text: Or finally, a third: Unlike CSLI, Location History can estimate a phone's elevation—so, for example, can tell whether someone has gone into a doctor's office on the first floor of a multi-story building, or a private apartment on the tenth.

data.text: - **Retrospective surveillance.**
Location History allows police to reconstruct people's comings and goings in any area, retrospectively and with no real effort.

citations.cited_text: And next, Location History also allows police officers to reconstruct "retrospective[ly]," and with no real effort, people's comings and goings in any area.

data.text: - **The user's own records.**
The records serve as a personal journal of a user's movements, which the user consults and can even edit.

citations.cited_text: The records thus serve as a personal journal of a user's movements, which that user consults (and even can edit) for his own purposes.

data.text: The majority likened them to emails, documents, photographs, or calendars that a user reasonably views as his own even if stored on Google's servers.

citations.cited_text: In that way, Location History resembles other private materials—think of emails, documents, photographs, or calendars—that even if stored on Google's servers, a user reasonably views as his own.

data.text:
### Arguments the majority rejected

- **Short duration.** The Government argued that a short window of location data is not a search. The majority responded that
the Government "is wrong about the incapacity of short-term location information to reveal private matters."

citations.cited_text: But to begin, the Government is wrong about the incapacity of short-term location information to reveal private matters.

data.text: It also said that
the sweep of the official invasion is not made less because the government, with hindsight, can pinpoint which few hours of movements it wants to review.

citations.cited_text: The sweep of the official invasion is not made less because the government, with the benefit of hindsight, can pinpoint exactly which few hours of movements it wants to review.

data.text: - ***Knotts*.** The majority said that
*Knotts* does not support the view that accessing two hours of Location History is not a search,

citations.cited_text: And contra the Government, Knotts does not support the view that accessing two hours of Location History is not a search.

data.text: noting that
the *Knotts* Court was explicit in keeping its holding cabined to rudimentary beeper technology.

citations.cited_text: The Court decided that the beeper did not turn the tail into a search, but was explicit in keeping its holding cabined to that rudimentary technology.

data.text: It also pointed out that
the surveillance in *Knotts* was confined to public roads.

citations.cited_text: And still another feature of Knotts makes it inapt here: that the surveillance there was confined to public roads.

data.text: Further,
"[w]hether something is a search does not depend on what it finds."

citations.cited_text: Whether something is a search does not depend on what it finds.

data.text: - **Third-party doctrine.** The majority said that
*Carpenter* refused to apply the third-party doctrine to CSLI, and no good reason exists to reach a different result for Location History.

citations.cited_text: The problem for the Government—and presumably the reason that its primary assertion in Carpenter has here become a secondary one—is that Carpenter refused to apply the third-party doctrine to CSLI, and no good reason exists to reach a different result for Location History.

data.text: It found that
both differentiating features highlighted in *Carpenter*—the revealing nature of the data and the fact that it is not truly shared—apply equally or better to Location History.

citations.cited_text: Both differentiating features highlighted in Carpenter apply equally or better to Location History.

data.text: - **Voluntary opt-in.** The majority noted that
Google prompts a user, repeatedly, to turn on the service.

citations.cited_text: As described earlier, Google prompts a user, and repeatedly, to turn on the service—when he sets up a Google account, when he sets up an Android phone, and when he sets up a Google app.

data.text: It added that
the prompt does not tell the user how frequently Google would record his location, how precise Location History can be, or how Google might give that information to the government.

citations.cited_text: By contrast, it does not tell him quite what he is signing up for: "how frequently Google would record [his] location"; "how precise Location History can be"; or how Google might give all that minute-by-minute location information to the government. 590 F. Supp. 3d, at 936; 136 F. 4th, at 128 (Wynn, J., concurring in judgment).

data.text: It also said that
a cell-phone user is not to be viewed as sharing private information with third parties just by doing the ordinary things cell-phone users do.

## What the Court left open

- **Reasonableness of the warrant.** The majority said that
whether the search here was reasonable, meaning that each of its steps was properly described with particularity and found to be supported by probable cause, is left to the Court of Appeals.

citations.cited_text: We leave to the Court of Appeals the further question whether, given the warrant issued, the search here was reasonable, meaning that each of its steps was properly described with particularity and found to be supported by probable cause.

data.text: It explained that
because the Fourth Circuit panel concluded that no search had occurred, it did not address whether the warrant validly authorized each stage.

citations.cited_text: Because the Fourth Circuit panel concluded that no search had occurred, it did not address whether the geofence warrant issued here validly authorized each stage of the search process.

data.text: The Court
vacated the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remanded for further proceedings.

citations.cited_text: For the reasons stated, we vacate the judgment of the Court of Appeals and remand the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

data.text: - **Good faith.** The Court had granted certiorari only on the Fourth Amendment question, and
does not address whether the good-faith exception to the exclusionary rule still allows admission of the Location History data.

citations.cited_text: In line with our grant of certiorari, we do not address whether the good-faith exception to the exclusionary rule still allows the admission of the Location History data in this case.

data.text: That question remains for the Fourth Circuit to consider anew.

citations.cited_text: That question remains for the Fourth Circuit to consider anew, gleaning anything it thinks relevant from our decision on the substantive Fourth Amendment issues.

data.text: - **Exigent circumstances.**
The decision "does not call into doubt, in such circumstances, a warrantless geofence search."

citations.cited_text: Today's decision does not call into doubt, in such circumstances, a warrantless geofence search.

data.text:
The majority did describe the standards the Fourth Circuit will apply:
- **Probable cause.**
A magistrate must always determine that there is a "fair probability that contraband or evidence of a crime will be found" in the place searched.

citations.cited_text: But a magistrate must always determine that there is a "fair probability that contraband or evidence of a crime will be found" in the place searched.

data.text: - **Particularity.**
That requirement typically looks to such matters as the geographic and durational expanse of the search,

citations.cited_text: That requirement typically looks to such matters as the geographic and durational expanse of the search.

data.text: and
it must take account of "particular factual contexts," including in surveillance cases the nature of the technology to be used.

citations.cited_text: And it too must take account of "particular factual contexts," including in surveillance cases the nature of the technology to be used.

data.text: The majority also described the parties' contentions.
Chatrie contends that at steps two and three the warrant left too much authority to police officers, and too little to the magistrate, to define the search's scope.

citations.cited_text: As to steps two and three, Chatrie contends that the warrant left too much authority to police officers—and too little to the magistrate—to define the search's scope and determine whether cause for it existed.

data.text: The Government urges that the discretion given to the officers at those steps fell within the bounds of reasonableness.

citations.cited_text: And the Government urges that the discretion given to the officers at steps two and three fell within the bounds of reasonableness.

data.text: The majority noted that
the warrant said very little about how officers would make their choices at the second and third steps.

citations.cited_text: As to how the officers would make their choices at the second and third steps—how they would pick the users subject to more intense scrutiny—the warrant said very little.

## Separate opinions

- **Justice Jackson, concurrence (joined by Justice Sotomayor).** She agreed that a search occurred but would have
gone further to explain that this search violated the Fourth Amendment.

citations.cited_text: I write separately because I would have gone further to explain that this search violated the Fourth Amendment.

data.text: In her view,
at a minimum the second and third stages did not satisfy the requirement of probable cause supporting a particularly described search.

citations.cited_text: In my view, it is clear that at a minimum the second and third stages of the search process here did not satisfy this foundational requirement.

data.text: She reasoned that
the warrant left "too much to the discretion of the officer[s] executing the order," giving them a "roving commission" to collect more data absent any justification to a magistrate.

citations.cited_text: In this way, the warrant left "too much to the discretion of the officer[s] executing the order," giving them a "roving commission" to collect more data absent any justification to a magistrate.

data.text:
This is a concurrence, not the Court's holding on reasonableness.
- **Justice Gorsuch, concurrence in the judgment (joined by no one).** He agreed that
the government's examination of Chatrie's Location History data amounted to a search,

citations.cited_text: I agree with the Court's judgment that the government's examination of Okello Chatrie's Location History data amounted to a search for purposes of the Fourth Amendment.

data.text: but
would reach that conclusion by a different route.

citations.cited_text: But respectfully, I would reach that conclusion by a different route.

data.text: He would not use *Katz* and the third-party doctrine. Instead,
he would ask whether Location History qualifies as one of Chatrie's papers or effects, and then whether the government searched them.

citations.cited_text: To decide whether the Fourth Amendment is in play, I would consult its terms, asking first whether Location History qualifies as one of Mr. Chatrie's papers or effects, and then asking whether the government searched those papers or effects.

data.text: He also questioned the majority's reasoning, asking
why tracking Chatrie's movements digitally over an hour or two invades his reasonable expectation of privacy when an officer tailing him for the same length of time would not.

citations.cited_text: Why does tracking Mr. Chatrie's movements digitally over an hour or two invade his reasonable expectation of privacy when an officer tailing him for the same length of time would not?

data.text: - **Justice Alito, dissent.** The dissent says the majority
"sheds *Carpenter*'s self-imposed boundaries and further destabilizes longstanding Fourth Amendment jurisprudence."

citations.cited_text: In doing so, the Court sheds Carpenter's self-imposed boundaries and further destabilizes longstanding Fourth Amendment jurisprudence.

that the "duration" of data obtained is too brief for a search to have happened,
